entry.title: The Great Miami Hurricane of 1926: 100 Years of Hurricane Forecasting and Research

media:group.media:title: The Great Miami Hurricane of 1926: 100 Years of Hurricane Forecasting and Research
media:group.media:description:
Predicting extreme weather events and warning the public was much more difficult before we had satellites, aircraft reconnaissance, computer models, radio, television, and the internet. In this talk, we will discuss the Great Miami Hurricane of 1926 and its effects, our understanding of weather and the state of forecasting at the time, what we learned from this event, and how we have advanced in the following 100 years.
Presenters: Dr. Sim Aberson and Dr. Jack Beven
This presentation is part of the NOAA Heritage Week 2026 Speaker Series.

media:group.media:title: Remembering Hurricane Katrina: 20 Years Later
media:group.media:description: 20 years ago, Hurricane Katrina tore through the southeastern United States, causing much destruction. This video features thoughts from NOAA staff who were involved in the forecasting and response. They share their memories of this tragic natural disaster, and the further forecasting advancements since then. Learn more about NOAA’s history at www.noaa.gov/heritage.

entry.title: Investing in America: NOAA's Science, Service and Stewardship in Action

media:group.media:title: Investing in America: NOAA's Science, Service and Stewardship in Action
media:group.media:description: From groundbreaking discoveries in the deepest depths of the ocean to pioneering satellite technology for severe weather monitoring, in the past four years, NOAA has introduced new innovations on air, land and sea to protect people, property and livelihoods across the nation. These historic investments in America’s climate resilience empowered local leaders and decision makers to understand, prepare for and mitigate climate impacts unique to their communities. Visit https://noaa.gov/2024report to learn more.

entry.title: NOAA provides vital navigation data in wake of Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse

media:group.media:title: NOAA provides vital navigation data in wake of Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse
media:group.media:description: Patapsco River, Baltimore, MD, Sunday, March 31, 2024: A Navigation Response Team from NOAA’s Office of Coast Survey conducts lidar and sonar operations at the site of the Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse to detect any obstructions and gather precise water depth and air gap measurements. This work provides data essential to establishing an alternate channel around the wreckage and determining what kinds of vessels can use it. For more details, please visit: https://www.noaa.gov/news/noaa-science-experts-assets-responding-247-to-francis-scott-key-bridge-disaster

entry.title: Xin Lan: Greenhouse Gas Scientist, NOAA Research Global Monitoring Laboratory

media:group.media:title: Xin Lan: Greenhouse Gas Scientist, NOAA Research Global Monitoring Laboratory
media:group.media:description:
Xin views Women’s History Month as a time for celebration and reflection, and an opportunity to remember that women are not treated equally throughout the world.
If given the opportunity to share advice with her younger self, she would say that despite what she was told by others, girls can grow up to be great scientists.

entry.title: Kayelyn Simmons: Oceanographer, NOAA Research Atlantic Oceanographic & Meteorological Laboratory

media:group.media:title: Kayelyn Simmons: Oceanographer, NOAA Research Atlantic Oceanographic & Meteorological Laboratory
media:group.media:description:
Kayelyn celebrates Women’s History Month by shopping at women-owned businesses and participating in a number of activities, including scuba diving, martial arts and spear fishing.
What advice would she give to her younger self? To have more confidence in her academic abilities.

entry.title: Ocean to Atmosphere: Research and Innovation at NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory.

media:group.media:title: Ocean to Atmosphere: Research and Innovation at NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory.
media:group.media:description:
NOAA’s Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory (PMEL) is a federal laboratory based in Seattle, Washington, with additional offices in Newport, Oregon. PMEL makes critical observations and conducts groundbreaking research to advance our knowledge of the global ocean and its interactions with the earth, atmosphere, ecosystems, and climate. These observations are used to improve weather and climate predictions, fisheries management, and coastal resilience. PMEL is a global leader in the development and deployment of innovative strategies for ocean observation.
Visit PMEL's YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/user/NOAAPMEL and the PMEL homepage: https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/ for more great content.
